claim: Optical stimulation of the mystacial pad in Emx1-Cre;Ai27D transgenic mice induces whisker movements due to activation of ChR2 expressed in muscles controlling retraction and protraction.
source: We discovered that optical stimulation of the mystacial pad in Emx1-Cre;Ai27D transgenic mice induces whisker movements due to activation of ChR2 expressed in muscles controlling retraction and protraction.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including histological analysis and videography.

claim: Optogenetic whisker pad stimulation evokes robust yet longer latency responses in primary somatosensory cortex (S1) compared to mechanical whisker stimulation in anesthetized mice.
source: Recordings from primary somatosensory cortex (S1) in anesthetized mice indicated that optogenetic whisker pad stimulation evokes robust yet longer latency responses than mechanical whisker stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing a 10.8 ± 0.1 ms longer latency for optogenetic stimulation compared to mechanical stimulation.

claim: In head-fixed mice trained to report optogenetic whisker pad stimulation, psychometric curves showed similar dependence on stimulus duration as evoked whisker movements and S1 activity.
source: In head-fixed mice trained to report optogenetic whisker pad stimulation, psychometric curves showed similar dependence on stimulus duration as evoked whisker movements and S1 activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data showing that Hit rate, whisker movement amplitude, and S1 responses all increase with stimulus duration in similar patterns.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of S1 in expert mice was sufficient to substitute for peripheral stimulation in the detection task.
source: Furthermore, optogenetic stimulation of S1 in expert mice was sufficient to substitute for peripheral stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data showing that lick rate in response to S1 stimulation was not significantly different from peripheral optogenetic stimulation.

claim: Whisker protractions evoked by optogenetic activation of whisker pad muscles result in cortical activity and sensory perception consistent with the coding of evoked whisker movements by reafferent sensory input.
source: We conclude that whisker protractions evoked by optogenetic activation of whisker pad muscles results in cortical activity and sensory perception, consistent with the coding of evoked whisker movements by reafferent sensory input.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the integration of multiple experimental findings including whisker movement characterization, S1 recordings, and behavioral detection.

claim: Active sensing involves the integration of internally generated motor commands with sensation of the external world.
source: Active sensing involves the integration of internally generated motor commands with sensation of the external world.
evidence: This is a general statement about active sensing that is established in the field.

claim: Rodents use their mystacial vibrissae (whiskers) to sample the immediate environment in rhythmic bouts of active self-generated whisker movements, called whisking.
source: In the rodent whisker system, which has been used extensively as an experimental model of active sensing, animals use their mystacial vibrissae (whiskers) to sample the immediate environment in rhythmic bouts of active self-generated whisker movements, called whisking (Kleinfeld et al., 2006; Brecht, 2007; Diamond et al., 2008; Prescott et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature in the field.

claim: A temporal sequence of extrinsic and intrinsic whisker pad muscle activation drives exploratory whisking: the extrinsic muscle M. nasolabialis profundis initiates the forward pad translation, and then the intrinsic 'sling' muscles that surround the base of each whisker follicle drive further protraction.
source: A temporal sequence of extrinsic and intrinsic whisker pad muscle activation drives exploratory whisking: the extrinsic muscle M. nasolabialis profundis initiates the forward pad translation, and then the intrinsic 'sling' muscles that surround the base of each whisker follicle drive further protraction (Dörfl, 1982; Berg and Kleinfeld, 2003; Hill et al., 2008; Bosman et al., 2011; Haidarliu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations describing the anatomy and physiology of whisker pad muscles.

claim: Sensory signals arising from whisker-object contact are transmitted through the infraorbital nerve to trigeminal ganglion, ventral-posterior medial (VPM) thalamus, and S1.
source: Sensory signals arising from whisker-object contact are transmitted through the infraorbital nerve to trigeminal ganglion, ventral-posterior medial (VPM) thalamus, and S1 (Petersen, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to established anatomical pathways in the whisker sensory system.

claim: Whisker pad muscles almost completely lack spindles, so proprioception is thought to play a minor role, if any, in determining whisker position in space.
source: Because whisker pad muscles almost completely lack spindles, proprioception is thought to play a minor role, if any, in determining whisker position in space.
evidence: This is a statement about the anatomical properties of whisker pad muscles and their functional implications.

claim: Sensations that arise from whisker self-motion – 'reafferent' signaling – is thought to play an important role in determining whisker position and object localization.
source: Instead, sensations that arise from whisker self-motion – 'reafferent' signaling – is thought to play an important role in determining whisker position and object localization (Kleinfeld and Deschênes, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to literature on reafferent signaling in the whisker system.

claim: Earlier studies suggested that reafferent signaling is encoded in parallel to afferent (touch-related) signals via posterior medial (POm) thalamus.
source: Although earlier studies suggested that reafferent signaling is encoded in parallel to afferent (touch-related) signals via posterior medial (POm) thalamus (Yu et al., 2006), recent evidence suggests that reafferent signaling is also processed along the same lemniscal (VPM-S1) pathway to cortex as afferent input from whisker-object contact (Moore et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Recent evidence suggests that reafferent signaling is also processed along the same lemniscal (VPM-S1) pathway to cortex as afferent input from whisker-object contact.
source: Although earlier studies suggested that reafferent signaling is encoded in parallel to afferent (touch-related) signals via posterior medial (POm) thalamus (Yu et al., 2006), recent evidence suggests that reafferent signaling is also processed along the same lemniscal (VPM-S1) pathway to cortex as afferent input from whisker-object contact (Moore et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: Many studies of reafferent sensory signaling have used an 'artificial whisking' paradigm to elicit whisker movements in anesthetized rodents by electrical stimulation of the buccal branch of the facial motor nerve.
source: Many studies of reafferent sensory signaling have used an 'artificial whisking' paradigm to elicit whisker movements in anesthetized rodents by electrical stimulation of the buccal branch of the facial motor nerve (Zucker and Welker, 1969; Brown and Waite, 1974; Szwed et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies using the artificial whisking paradigm.

claim: Artificial whisking produces whisker protractions with amplitude and frequency that can be well controlled experimentally.
source: Artificial whisking produces whisker protractions with amplitude and frequency that can be well controlled experimentally.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of the artificial whisking technique.

claim: The artificial whisking paradigm has drawbacks, including the necessity to perform experiments in anesthetized subjects, which makes it difficult to relate reafferent signaling to behavior.
source: This paradigm has drawbacks, however, including the necessity to perform experiments in anesthetized subjects, which makes it difficult to relate reafferent signaling to behavior; and the inability to stimulate certain muscle groups, which means that only whisker protractions, not retractions, can be evoked.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the artificial whisking technique.

claim: The artificial whisking paradigm has the drawback of inability to stimulate certain muscle groups, which means that only whisker protractions, not retractions, can be evoked.
source: This paradigm has drawbacks, however, including the necessity to perform experiments in anesthetized subjects, which makes it difficult to relate reafferent signaling to behavior; and the inability to stimulate certain muscle groups, which means that only whisker protractions, not retractions, can be evoked.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the artificial whisking technique.

claim: Optogenetic studies of motor nerves and muscles have used the hindlimb as a model system.
source: Recently, optogenetic studies of motor nerves and muscles have used the hindlimb as a model system (Liske et al., 2013; Towne et al., 2013; Bryson et al., 2014; Magown et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies using optogenetics in the hindlimb.

claim: Various central elements of the whisker system have been targeted for optical control in behaving mice.
source: While various central elements of the whisker system have been targeted for optical control in behaving mice (Poulet et al., 2012; O'Connor et al., 2013; Sachidhanandam et al., 2013; Matyas et al., 2010), peripheral optogenetic stimulation have not been used to investigate control of whisker movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies using optogenetics in central whisker system structures.

claim: Peripheral optogenetic stimulation has not been used to investigate control of whisker movements prior to this study.
source: While various central elements of the whisker system have been targeted for optical control in behaving mice (Poulet et al., 2012; O'Connor et al., 2013; Sachidhanandam et al., 2013; Matyas et al., 2010), peripheral optogenetic stimulation have not been used to investigate control of whisker movements.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current study's approach.

claim: The direction of whisker movement evoked by optogenetic stimulation depends on the location of the light spot on the whisker pad.
source: The direction of movement depended on the location of the spot, such that illumination of the rostral pad resulted in whisker protraction, while illumination of the caudal-inferior pad resulted in whisker retraction (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating different movement directions based on stimulation location.

claim: Illumination of the rostral pad results in whisker protraction.
source: The direction of movement depended on the location of the spot, such that illumination of the rostral pad resulted in whisker protraction, while illumination of the caudal-inferior pad resulted in whisker retraction (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Illumination of the caudal-inferior pad results in whisker retraction.
source: The direction of movement depended on the location of the spot, such that illumination of the rostral pad resulted in whisker protraction, while illumination of the caudal-inferior pad resulted in whisker retraction (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Stimulation at some locations elicited more complex combinations of protractions and retractions from individual whiskers.
source: Stimulation at some locations elicited more complex combinations of protractions and retractions from individual whiskers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; see also Video 1, Video 2, Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and videos.

claim: Regional variations in light-evoked protraction and retraction were qualitatively similar in 5 of 5 mice tested.
source: These regional variations in light-evoked protraction and retraction were qualitatively similar in 5 of 5 mice tested.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations across multiple subjects.

claim: Intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the whisker pad exhibit tdTomato fluorescence in Emx1-Cre;Ai27D mice.
source: Indeed, analysis of the native fluorescence of the ChR2/tdTomato fusion protein in sections of the whisker pad revealed tdTomato expression in intrinsic and extrinsic whisker pad muscles (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Intrinsic muscles appear on both superior and inferior sides of the follicle in coronal sections, and on the rostral side in transverse sections, consistent with their sling-like morphology.
source: Intrinsic muscles appeared on both superior and inferior sides of the follicle in coronal sections, and on the rostral side in transverse sections (Figure 1C1, C2), consistent with their sling-like morphology (Dörfl, 1982; Haidarliu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological observations in Figure 1C1 and C2, and is consistent with cited literature on muscle morphology.

claim: No fluorescence was evident in the infraorbital (sensory) nerve in Emx1-Cre;Ai27D mice.
source: No fluorescence was evident in the infraorbital (sensory) nerve (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Fluorescence intensity was highest in intrinsic sling muscles, followed by the deep extrinsic retractor muscle, and lastly the superficial extrinsic protractor muscle.
source: Comparison of fluorescence intensity indicated the highest intensity in intrinsic sling muscles, followed by the deep extrinsic retractor muscle (pars maxillaris superficialis and pars maxillaris profunda of M. nasolabialis profundus), and lastly the superficial extrinsic protractor muscle (the pars media superior and pars media inferior of M. nasolabialis profundus,) (F(2,6) = 57.66, p=0.0001, repeated measures ANOVA followed by paired contrasts; p=0.0004 comparing external extrinsic and intrinsic, p=0.0086 comparing external extrinsic and internal extrinsic, p=0.0341 comparing intrinsic and internal extrinsic; n=4 follicles from one mouse) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 1D with statistical analysis.

claim: Light-evoked whisker movements in Emx1-Cre;Ai27D mice arise from activation of ChR2 expressed in extrinsic and intrinsic whisker pad muscles.
source: These results indicate that light-evoked whisker movements in Emx1-Cre;Ai27D mice arise from activation of ChR2 expressed in extrinsic and intrinsic whisker pad muscles.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the histological data showing ChR2 expression in muscles and the functional data showing light-evoked movements.

claim: The amplitude of whisker protraction in response to a 50 ms light pulse of increasing intensity (range, 1.3–10.3 mW) increased approximately linearly to a maximum amplitude of 11.4 ± 1.2 degrees.
source: The amplitude of whisker protraction in response to a 50 ms light pulse of increasing intensity (range, 1.3–10.3 mW) increased approximately linearly to a maximum amplitude of 11.4 ± 1.2 degrees (mean ± SEM, n = 4 mice; maximum 14.8 degrees in one mouse; Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements of whisker movements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In 2 of 4 mice, the angle change appeared to saturate at less than maximal power (8.37 and 9.94 mW, respectively).
source: In 2 of 4 mice, the angle change appeared to saturate at less than maximal power (8.37 and 9.94 mW, respectively).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data on intensity-response relationships.

claim: The average latency of optogenetically evoked whisker movement was 13.5 ± 0.3 ms.
source: The average latency of optogenetically evoked whisker movement was 13.5 ± 0.3 ms (mean ± SEM, n = 4 mice; threshold defined as 10% of the maximum peak) and was not affected by stimulus duration.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements of movement latency.

claim: The latency of optogenetically evoked whisker movement was not affected by stimulus duration.
source: The average latency of optogenetically evoked whisker movement was 13.5 ± 0.3 ms (mean ± SEM, n = 4 mice; threshold defined as 10% of the maximum peak) and was not affected by stimulus duration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations across different stimulus durations.

claim: Whisker protraction angle increased with the duration of the optical stimulus, saturating with durations longer than approximately 60 ms.
source: Whisker protraction angle increased with the duration of the optical stimulus, saturating with durations longer than approximately 60 ms (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: At frequencies greater than 30 Hz, individual evoked movements were no longer discernible.
source: At frequencies greater than 30 Hz, individual evoked movements were no longer discernible, although the envelope of the angle change continued to show adaptation up to 45 Hz and became similar to movements elicited by constant prolonged light steps (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations of whisker movements at different stimulation frequencies.

claim: Optogenetically evoked whisker protractions show activation and adaptation over a behaviorally relevant range of frequencies.
source: These data indicate that optogenetically evoked whisker protractions show activation and adaptation over a behaviorally relevant range of frequencies.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the frequency-response data showing adaptation patterns.

claim: Spiking activity and LFP amplitude increased with the duration of peripheral optogenetic stimulation.
source: Spiking activity and LFP amplitude increased with the duration of peripheral optogenetic stimulation (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Spike count and LFP amplitude increase steeply with light pulse duration from 1–20 ms, and moderately between 20–100 ms.
source: Plotting the responses normalized to the maximum response in each mouse indicated that spike count and LFP amplitude increase steeply with light pulse duration from 1–20 ms, and moderately between 20–100 ms (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by normalized response data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The spike number and LFP amplitude evoked by peripheral optogenetic stimulation were on average similar to those evoked by mechanical whisker deflection.
source: The spike number and LFP amplitude evoked by peripheral optogenetic stimulation were on average similar to those evoked by mechanical whisker deflection (peak spike number per stimulus in 10 ms bin: 3.5 ± 0.2 mechanical, 3.2 ± 1.1 optical; LFP peak amplitude: −168.5 ± 24.7 µV mechanical, 159.66 ± 45.1 µV optical).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative comparison of electrophysiological responses to different stimulation types.

claim: The response latency determined from LFP recordings was 10.8 ± 0.1 ms longer for peripheral optogenetic stimulation compared to mechanical whisker stimulation.
source: Notably, the response latency determined from LFP recordings was 10.8 ± 0.1 ms longer for peripheral optogenetic stimulation compared to mechanical whisker stimulation (p<1x10-5 in n = 3/3 mice; paired t-tests; 13–39 trials per mouse) (Figure 3C, inset; Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative latency measurements with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C and E.

claim: The longer latency in S1 for peripheral optogenetic stimulation can likely be attributed to the 11.9 ± 0.8 ms delay associated with the initiation of evoked whisker movement.
source: These results suggest that the longer latency in S1 for peripheral optogenetic stimulation can likely be attributed to the 11.9 ± 0.8 ms delay associated with the initiation of evoked whisker movement (Figure 2B; value from 9.3 mW intensity), and that sensory signals arrive rapidly in S1once whisker movement is initiated.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the latency difference with the whisker movement initiation delay.

claim: Sensory signals arrive rapidly in S1 once whisker movement is initiated.
source: These results suggest that the longer latency in S1 for peripheral optogenetic stimulation can likely be attributed to the 11.9 ± 0.8 ms delay associated with the initiation of evoked whisker movement (Figure 2B; value from 9.3 mW intensity), and that sensory signals arrive rapidly in S1once whisker movement is initiated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the latency data comparing optogenetic and mechanical stimulation.

claim: The electrophysiological results are consistent with histological data suggesting that ChR2 is expressed in muscle and absent from sensory nerve.
source: These results are consistent with our histological data suggesting that ChR2 is expressed in muscle and absent from sensory nerve (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the electrophysiological findings with the histological observations.

claim: Two of four mice learned the behavioral detection task (d'>1) within 4 sessions.
source: Two of four mice learned the task (d'>1) within 4 sessions (2 sessions per day, 125 trials per session), showing maintained Hit rate with relatively low FA rate (FA rate < 0.3).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral performance data during training.

claim: Two of four mice learned the behavioral detection task only after introducing 2 M salt water solution as additional punishment for licking during FA trials.
source: The other two mice learned only after introducing 2 M salt water solution as additional punishment for licking during FA trials.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral training data.

claim: Behavioral performance improved via a maintained high Hit rate and a decrease in FA rate, resulting in an increase in d' from 0.7 ± 0.1 to 2.3 ± 0.4 over the course of training.
source: Overall, behavioral performance improved via a maintained high Hit rate and a decrease in FA rate, resulting in an increase in d' from 0.7 ± 0.1 to 2.3 ± 0.4 (mean ± SEM; p = 0.017, paired t-test; n = 4 mice) over the course of training (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative behavioral performance data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Hit rate fell to chance levels with stimuli shorter than 5 ms in expert mice performing the detection task.
source: We found that Hit rate fell to chance levels with stimuli shorter than 5 ms (Figure 4C), defining a lower limit of optical stimulation necessary for behavioral detection.
evidence: This claim is supported by psychometric data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The behaviorally measured detection threshold is similar to the threshold for evoked whisker movements and S1 activity measured in anesthetized mice.
source: Note that this behaviorally measured detection threshold is similar to the threshold for evoked whisker movements (Figure 2C) and S1 activity (Figure 3D) measured in anesthetized mice.
evidence: This is a comparison of behavioral thresholds with physiological measurements.

claim: Lick rate for visual catch trials was 0.37 ± 0.07 compared to 0.87 ± 0.04 for peripheral optogenetic stimulation.
source: Lick rate for visual catch trials was 0.37 ± 0.07 compared to 0.87 ± 0.04 for peripheral optogenetic stimulation (328 peripheral stimulation trials, 75 visual catch trials in 6 sessions from n = 2 mice) (Figure 4D), suggesting that visual stimulation was not a salient cue involved in performance of the peripheral optogenetic detection task.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data comparing responses to different stimulation types shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Visual stimulation was not a salient cue involved in performance of the peripheral optogenetic detection task.
source: Lick rate for visual catch trials was 0.37 ± 0.07 compared to 0.87 ± 0.04 for peripheral optogenetic stimulation (328 peripheral stimulation trials, 75 visual catch trials in 6 sessions from n = 2 mice) (Figure 4D), suggesting that visual stimulation was not a salient cue involved in performance of the peripheral optogenetic detection task.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low lick rate for visual catch trials compared to peripheral stimulation.

claim: In expert mice, lick rate in response to S1 stimulation (100 ms) was not significantly different compared to peripheral optogenetic stimulation (100 ms).
source: In expert mice, lick rate in response to S1 stimulation (100 ms) was not significantly different compared to peripheral optogenetic stimulation (100 ms), but was significantly greater than FA lick rate (F(2,6) = 17.62, p=0.0031, repeated measures ANOVA followed by paired contrasts; p=0.43072 comparing peripheral and S1 stimulation, p=0.0238 comparing S1 stimulation and FA, p=0.016 comparing peripheral stimulation and FA; 160 peripheral stimulation trials, 156 S1 simulation trials, 160 FA trials in 2 sessions from n = 4 mice) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Lick rate in response to S1 stimulation was significantly greater than FA lick rate.
source: In expert mice, lick rate in response to S1 stimulation (100 ms) was not significantly different compared to peripheral optogenetic stimulation (100 ms), but was significantly greater than FA lick rate (F(2,6) = 17.62, p=0.0031, repeated measures ANOVA followed by paired contrasts; p=0.43072 comparing peripheral and S1 stimulation, p=0.0238 comparing S1 stimulation and FA, p=0.016 comparing peripheral stimulation and FA; 160 peripheral stimulation trials, 156 S1 simulation trials, 160 FA trials in 2 sessions from n = 4 mice) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of S1 is sufficient to drive sensory detection in mice that were trained to detect peripheral optogenetic stimulation.
source: These results indicate that optogenetic stimulation of S1 is sufficient to drive sensory detection in mice that were trained to detect peripheral optogenetic stimulation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the behavioral data showing similar lick rates for S1 and peripheral stimulation.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of mystacial pad muscles in Emx1-Cre;Ai27D mice induces whisker movements linked to ChR2 expression in intrinsic and extrinsic muscles.
source: We found that optogenetic stimulation of mystacial pad muscles in Emx1-Cre;Ai27D mice induces whisker movements linked to ChR2 expression in intrinsic and extrinsic muscles, and that mice can readily report sensory perception associated with peripheral optogenetic stimulation.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings supported by multiple experiments.

claim: Mice can readily report sensory perception associated with peripheral optogenetic stimulation.
source: We found that optogenetic stimulation of mystacial pad muscles in Emx1-Cre;Ai27D mice induces whisker movements linked to ChR2 expression in intrinsic and extrinsic muscles, and that mice can readily report sensory perception associated with peripheral optogenetic stimulation.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the behavioral findings.

claim: Combined cortical stimulation experiments illustrated the utility of Emx1-Cre;Ai27D mice for optogenetic investigation of both peripheral and central excitable cells.
source: Combined cortical stimulation experiments illustrated the utility of Emx1-Cre;Ai27D mice for optogenetic investigation of both peripheral and central excitable cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the successful use of both peripheral and central optogenetic stimulation in the same mice.

claim: A practical benefit of peripheral expression in Emx1-Cre;Ai27D mice is that transgene transmission to offspring can be inferred simply by visual inspection under fluorescence instead of traditional DNA genotyping.
source: A practical benefit of peripheral expression worth mentioning is that transgene transmission to offspring can be inferred simply by visual inspection under fluorescence instead of traditional DNA genotyping.
evidence: This is a practical observation about the utility of peripheral fluorescence expression.

claim: Peripheral Cre expression is known in other Cre driver lines commonly used for neurobiological studies of the central nervous system.
source: Peripheral Cre expression is known in other Cre driver lines commonly used for neurobiological studies of the central nervous system.
evidence: This is a statement about the broader context of Cre driver lines.

claim: Chat-Cre, often used to target cholinergic neurons of basal forebrain, also drives expression in motoneurons.
source: For example, Chat-Cre, often used to target cholinergic neurons of basal forebrain (Eggermann et al., 2014; Hangya et al., 2015) also drives expression in motoneurons (Gong et al., 2007; Takatoh et al., 2013);
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies documenting Chat-Cre expression patterns.

claim: PV-Cre, often used to target a class of central GABAergic interneurons, also expresses in proprioceptive neurons of the dorsal root ganglion, sensory neurons of trigeminal ganglion, and fast-twitch skeletal muscle fibers.
source: PV-Cre, often used to target a class of central GABAergic interneurons (Cardin et al., 2009; Sohal et al., 2009; Gentet et al., 2010), also expresses in proprioceptive neurons of the dorsal root ganglion (Hippenmeyer et al., 2005), sensory neurons of trigeminal ganglion (Sakurai et al., 2013), and fast-twitch skeletal muscle fibers (Chakkalakal et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations documenting PV-Cre expression in various tissues.

claim: Many Cre driver lines have been developed exclusively for investigation of the peripheral nervous system and muscle.
source: It should be noted that, in addition to such incidental central/peripheral expression, many other Cre driver lines have been developed exclusively for investigation of the peripheral nervous system (da Silva et al., 2011; Rutlin et al., 2014) and muscle (Chen et al., 2005; Li et al., 2005; Chakkalakal et al., 2012; Magown et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies developing and using peripheral-specific Cre lines.

claim: Whisker movements in Emx1-Cre;Ai27D mice are induced by direct stimulation of the ChR2-expressing muscle instead of the innervating facial nerve.
source: Whisker movements in Emx1-Cre;Ai27D mice are induced by direct stimulation of the ChR2-expressing muscle instead of the innervating facial nerve.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the histological data showing ChR2 expression in muscle but not nerve.

claim: Direct muscle stimulation could be an advantage for therapeutic models in which denervation or motoneuron degeneration has occurred.
source: However, direct muscle stimulation could be an advantage for therapeutic models in which denervation or motoneuron degeneration has occurred (Magown et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications, supported by a citation.

claim: ChR2 expression in muscle allows an extended repertoire of whisker movements compared to artificial whisking, including both optically evoked retractions and protractions.
source: ChR2 expression in muscle also allows an extended repertoire of whisker movements compared to artificial whisking, including both optically evoked retractions and protractions.
evidence: This is a comparison of the capabilities of optogenetic muscle stimulation versus artificial whisking.

claim: Light-evoked protractions involve activation of intrinsic muscles, as well as the pars media superior and pars media inferior of the M. nasolabialis profundus.
source: Our results, in accordance with previous anatomical and physiological studies (Dörfl, 1982; Dörfl, 1985; Berg and Kleinfeld, 2003; Hill et al., 2008; Haidarliu et al., 2010; 2015), suggest that light-evoked protractions involve activation of intrinsic muscles, as well as the pars media superior and pars media inferior of the M. nasolabialis profundus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current histological data and cited literature on muscle anatomy and function.

claim: Retractions involve activation of the (deep) pars maxillaris superficialis and pars maxillaris profunda of the M. nasolabialis profundus.
source: Retractions involve activation of the (deep) pars maxillaris superficialis and pars maxillaris profunda of the M. nasolabialis profundus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the histological data showing ChR2 expression in these muscles and the observed retraction movements.

claim: The relative contribution of activation of intrinsic versus extrinsic muscles to evoked whisker protractions remains unclear.
source: Because ChR2 is expressed in both muscle types, the relative contribution of activation of intrinsic versus extrinsic muscles to evoked whisker protractions remains unclear.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in the current study.

claim: Optical stimulation at the rostral whisker pad could favor protraction because of the morphology of the muscles along the surface of the pad, specifically the caudal-to-rostral tapered morphology of the deep retraction muscles.
source: Optical stimulation at the rostral whisker pad could favor protraction because of the morphology of the muscles along the surface of the pad, specifically the caudal-to-rostral tapered morphology of the deep retraction muscles (pars maxillaris superficialis and pars maxillaris profunda) (Haidarliu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on muscle anatomy cited from the literature.

claim: Studies using artificial whisking in rats report amplitudes of up to 20 degrees.
source: The maximum amplitude of optogenetically evoked protractions that we found was 11.4 degrees on average in four mice (largest individual mouse average, 14.8 degrees, Figure 2; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1for single trial examples from multiple tracked whiskers), while studies using artificial whisking in rats report amplitudes of up to 20 degrees (Yu et al., 2006; Castro-Alamancos and Bezdudnaya, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies using artificial whisking.

claim: One possible explanation for smaller amplitude in optogenetic stimulation is that the excitation light was restricted to a 2–3 mm diameter spot on the whisker pad, while nerve stimulation evokes widespread muscle activation via acetylcholine release throughout the whisker pad.
source: One possible explanation is that the excitation light was restricted to a 2–3 mm diameter spot on the whisker pad, while nerve stimulation evokes widespread muscle activation via acetylcholine release throughout the whisker pad.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed difference in movement amplitude.

claim: Optogenetically evoked protractions showed stronger frequency adaptation than reported for artificial whisking.
source: We also note that optogenetically evoked protractions showed stronger frequency adaptation than reported for artificial whisking.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings with literature on artificial whisking.

claim: 100 Hz electrical nerve stimulation (artificial whisking) results in sustained whisker protraction for up to 1 s.
source: We found strong adaptation over a stimulus frequency range of 2 to 28 Hz (Figure 2D), whereas 100 Hz electrical nerve stimulation (artificial whisking) results in sustained whisker protraction for up to 1 s (Castro-Alamancos and Bezdudnaya, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on artificial whisking.

claim: The adaptation effects observed could be explained by potential differences in muscle groups recruited by optogenetic stimulation in Emx1-Cre;Ai27D mice compared to artificial whisking.
source: This could be explained by potential differences in muscle groups recruited by optogenetic stimulation in Emx1-Cre;Ai27D mice compared to artificial whisking.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed adaptation.

claim: It is unlikely that desensitization of ChR2-mediated currents accounts for the adaptation effects measured.
source: It is unlikely that desensitization of ChR2-mediated currents accounts for the adaptation effects we measured, since optogenetic stimulation of hindlimb muscles produces non-adapting contractions with pulse durations up to 1 s (Magown et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study showing non-adapting optogenetic muscle contractions in the hindlimb.

claim: Intrinsic muscles of the whisker pad are rapidly fatiguing because they consist almost exclusively of type 2B muscle fibers.
source: Intrinsic muscles of the whisker pad are rapidly fatiguing because they consist almost exclusively of type 2B muscle fibers (Jin et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on muscle fiber composition.

claim: The fiber composition of extrinsic muscles is less clear, but appears to be of mixed fiber type.
source: The fiber composition of extrinsic muscles is less clear, but appears to be of mixed fiber type (Jin et al., 2004; Grant et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on muscle fiber composition.

claim: The results showing strong adaptation are consistent with activation of rapidly fatiguing muscle fibers by optogenetic stimulation.
source: Our results showing strong adaptation are consistent with activation of rapidly fatiguing muscle fibers by optogenetic stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the observed adaptation with known muscle fiber properties.

claim: During natural whisking, reafferent input arises from the whiskers moving through space.
source: During natural whisking, reafferent input arises from the whiskers moving through space and, because rodents mostly lack proprioceptors in whisker pad muscles (Moore et al., 2015), reafferent signaling is considered important for encoding whisker position and locating objects in space (Kleinfeld and Deschênes, 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of reafferent input during whisking.

source: During natural whisking, reafferent input arises from the whiskers moving through space and, because rodents mostly lack proprioceptors in whisker pad muscles (Moore et al., 2015), reafferent signaling is considered important for encoding whisker position and locating objects in space (Kleinfeld and Deschênes, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on proprioception in whisker muscles.

source: It should be noted that two mice required introduction of salt water punishment to reduce impulsive responding, as has been used in other types of Go/NoGo tasks (Rebello et al., 2014), and that d' remained below that observed in other studies due to a sustained FA rate of approximately 0.2 (Huber et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2015).

claim: The whisker must move before sensory signals arrive in cortex during optogenetic stimulation.
source: Electrophysiological recordings from S1 showed that the latency was approximately 10 ms longer for optogenetically compared to mechanically evoked responses (Figure 3C,E), suggesting that the whisker must move before sensory signals arrive in cortex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the latency difference between optogenetic and mechanical stimulation.

claim: Mice were not responding to visual aspects of optogenetic stimulation in the behavioral task.
source: Visual stimulation was not sufficient to substitute for peripheral stimulation in expert mice performing the detection task, suggesting that mice were not responding to visual aspects of optogenetic stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low lick rate for visual catch trials.

claim: S1 is involved in perception of reafferent sensory signals.
source: Optogenetic stimulation of S1 was sufficient to substitute for peripheral optogenetic stimulation in the detection task (whereas naïve mice did not respond to S1 stimulation; data not shown), suggesting that S1 is involved in perception of reafferent sensory signals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral data showing that S1 stimulation can substitute for peripheral stimulation.

claim: The whisker movements elicited by optogenetic activation of muscles in the whisker pad lead to sensory perception through reafferent sensory signaling.
source: We conclude that the whisker movements elicited by optogenetic activation of muscles in the whisker pad lead to sensory perception through reafferent sensory signaling.
